claims.text: Uniformly incorporating graphene nanoplatelets into the HEA matrix will promote formation of an in situ tribolayer during sliding.
The resulting tribolayer will be resilient and adaptive.
The graphene-derived tribolayer will reduce the coefficient of friction.
The graphene-derived tribolayer will reduce the wear rate.
The reductions in friction and wear will persist from sub-ambient or cryogenic temperatures to high service temperatures.
The untreated HEA exhibits relatively high friction over a broad temperature range.
The untreated HEA exhibits relatively high wear over a broad temperature range.
The proposed intervention is uniform incorporation of graphene nanoplatelets into the bulk HEA during synthesis.
Sliding will produce a nanoscale graphene-containing lubricious layer at the contact interface.
Graphene acts as a solid lubricant because of its low shear strength.
Mechanical stress and local sliding-induced heating will trigger graphene nanoplatelet migration toward the contact surfaces.
Migrated graphene nanoplatelets will align and form a continuous, self-adapting tribolayer.
The tribolayer will protect the underlying HEA from wear.
Graphene incorporation will reduce the coefficient of friction by 20–40% relative to the untreated HEA.
Graphene incorporation will reduce the wear rate by 20–40% relative to the untreated HEA.
The improvement requires graphene to remain uniformly dispersed and undegraded after processing.
Extreme thermal cycling may limit the effectiveness of the graphene modification.
Oxidation or agglomeration of graphene may limit the effectiveness of the modification.
Prior work directly integrating graphene into bulk HEAs is limited.
The hypothesis is to be rejected if both tribological metrics do not improve by at least 20% across the tested temperature range, or if no protective tribolayer is observed.
